title: Deduplicate Event Stream
summary: Collapse at-least-once delivered events into one record per event id, keeping the latest version.

stages.title: Latest version wins
stages.requirement:
Our queue delivers events **at least once**, so the same event can arrive several times with
updated payloads. Each event is a dict with `"id"` (str), `"version"` (int) and other fields.

Write `dedupe(events)` returning one event per `id`:

- Keep the event with the **highest `version`**. If versions tie, keep the one that arrived
  **last**.
- Order the output by when each `id` was **first** seen.
- Return the original dict objects, and don't mutate the input.

```python
dedupe([
    {"id": "a", "version": 1, "v": "x"},
    {"id": "b", "version": 1, "v": "y"},
    {"id": "a", "version": 2, "v": "z"},
])
# -> [{"id": "a", "version": 2, "v": "z"}, {"id": "b", "version": 1, "v": "y"}]
```

hints: You need two things per id: the best event so far, and when the id first appeared.
A dict preserves insertion order, so inserting each id once (on first sight) and then replacing its value keeps the right order.
Replace the stored event when the new version is `>=` the stored one. `>=` makes the last arrival win ties.

solution.explanation:
Python dicts keep keys in insertion order, and reassigning an existing key keeps its
position. So one dict gives both "first appearance order" and "best version per id". The
`>=` comparison means later arrivals win ties. Returning the stored references (no copies)
satisfies the identity requirement and leaves the input untouched.
